case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Left lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forPAX8,TTF-1, thyroglobulin, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative results for napsin A. Right lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forTTF-1, napsin A, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative forPAX8and thyroglobulin. Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). The right lung lobectomy revealed a crowded cribriform glandular arrangement with luminal mucin, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and vesiculated nuclear chromatin (Figure, B).

case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.
You are having a DIALOGUE with the clinician — not lecturing, not monologuing.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

[Interaction Guidelines]
1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Left lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forPAX8,TTF-1, thyroglobulin, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative results for napsin A. Right lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forTTF-1, napsin A, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative forPAX8and thyroglobulin. Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). The right lung lobectomy revealed a crowded cribriform glandular arrangement with luminal mucin, eosinophilic cytoplasm, and vesiculated nuclear chromatin (Figure, B).

case_info.scenario: A 66-year-old man initially presented to his primary care physician with a persistent cough. A noncontrast chest computed tomography (CT) scan revealed multiple bilateral pulmonary nodules. Subsequent positron emission tomography/CT revealed intrathoracic lymphadenopathy, partially calcified left supraclavicular lymph node, left thyroid nodule, and left level IV neck lymph nodes with calcifications. Mutual analysis of the supraclavicular and left neck lymph node biopsies reported anNCOA4:RETgene fusion, but noBRAF V600Evariant. Left lower lung lobectomy showed tumor cells positive forPAX8,TTF-1, thyroglobulin, andNCOA4:RETgene fusion and negative results for napsin A. Histologically, the supraclavicular lymph node revealed a papillary architecture with nuclear pseudoinclusions and grooves that was identical to the left lung lobectomy (Figure, A). case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.

case_info.caption: A, Supraclavicular lymph node biopsy showing a papillary, hyalinized fibrotic nodule with engorged vasculature (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2). B, Right lung lobectomy specimen demonstrating a solid cribriform pattern with eosinophilic cytoplasm (hematoxylin-eosin; original magnification ×2).
case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. case_info.explanation: B. Two synchronous primary cancers (lung and thyroid) sharing a common somatic or germline variant This case represents a unique scenario in which 2 histologically unrelated tumors shared a common actionable molecular target, underscoring a shared therapeutic vulnerability.1,2Although both tumors harbored RET rearrangements, they are histologically and molecularly distinct, arising from different cellular lineages: thyroid follicular epithelium in papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) and respiratory epithelium in lung adenocarcinoma.3RET fusions, includingNCOA4:RET, typically function as mutually exclusive oncogenic drivers, rarely cooccurring with other alterations, thereby supporting the independent clonal origin of each malignancy.4The presence of RET fusions is confirmed by next-generation sequencing, with RNA-based platforms offering the highest sensitivity for detecting RET rearrangements across tumor types.1Histologic and immunophenotypic examination of available specimens distinguishes them as separate primary tumors, excluding the possibility of a single metastatic process (A and C). Moreover, metastatic medullary thyroid carcinoma is unlikely, as the tumor’s immunohistochemistry profile, which was positive forPAX8,TTF-1, and thyroglobulin and had an absence of calcitonin, was inconsistent with medullary differentiation (D). RET is a receptor tyrosine kinase that plays a pivotal role in cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival.5Oncogenic RET fusions, such asNCOA4:RET, result in ligand-independent dimerization and activation of downstream signaling pathways, including MAPK and PI3K-AKT, promoting tumorigenesis.5RET alterations are clinically relevant in multiple cancers, occurring in 10% to 20% of PTCs and in 1% to 2% of non–small cell lung cancers (NSCLC).5RET fusions have also been detected in colorectal, pancreatic, and breast cancers, underscoring their tumor-agnostic therapeutic potential.1 CCDC6:RETandNCOA4:RETare most observed in PTC, whileKIF5B:RETpredominates in lung adenocarcinoma.1,6,7The identification of anNCOA4:RETfusion in thyroid and lung tumors is unusual and supports the diagnosis of 2 independent primary tumors rather than metastasis. Mechanistically, theNCOA4:RETfusion retains the RET tyrosine kinase domain fused to theNCOA4coiled-coil domain, leading to constitutive kinase activation.3,5Although this fusion has been described in thyroid and colorectal cancers, its occurrence in lung adenocarcinoma is uncommon, making this case clinically significant and molecularly unique.1 Multiple primary cancers occur in approximately 2% to 17% of patients with cancer, with prevalence associated with population characteristics and surveillance duration.8Distinguishing synchronous primaries from metastatic disease can be diagnostically challenging and necessitates a comprehensive evaluation, including histologic, immunohistochemical, and molecular analyses.8Misclassification may occur when shared genetic alterations are incorrectly interpreted as evidence of metastasis.8However, most multiprimary cancers exhibit distinct oncogenic drivers, indicating independent clonal events. Rarely, synchronous tumors share an actionable alteration, such as an RET fusion, which is thought to reflect genomic convergence rather than germline predisposition.8Accurate classification is critical given its implications for staging, prognosis, and therapeutic strategy. Selpercatinib, a kinase inhibitor of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase, has demonstrated clinical efficacy, with an objective response rate (ORR) of 64% in patients with RET fusion–positive NSCLC and an ORR of 79% in RET-positive thyroid cancers.9,10These findings informed its US Food and Drug Administration approval for RET fusion–positive NSCLC and thyroid carcinoma, and more recently for tumor-agnostic use in RET fusion–positive solid tumors.9Durable responses have been observed even in patients previously treated with multiple lines of therapy, highlighting its role as a highly effective and targeted systemic option across a spectrum of RET-driven cancers.10This patient underwent bilateral lower lung lobectomy, right middle lung lobe wedge resection, and total thyroidectomy with left neck dissection, followed by radioactive iodine therapy and selpercatinib initiation. Both tumors responded favorably to selpercatinib, reinforcing the tumor-agnostic utility of RET-directed therapy.9A pericolonic lesion is under evaluation to determine if it is metastatic or a third primary. As of last follow-up, the patient was continuing to take selpercatinib and be closely monitored by the interdisciplinary cancer care team.
